title: Level 2 Chemistry: Properties of Selected Organic Compounds -- 2025
subject: chemistry

questions.text:
Six organic compounds are given in the table below.

Complete the table by drawing the structure or giving the IUPAC (systematic) name.

| Compound | Structure | Name |
|---|---|---|
| A | (blank) | butanamine |
| B | Cl-C-H with Cl on top and bottom (CHCl2) | (blank) |
| C | (blank) | 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid |
| D | H-C-C-C-C=C-C-H with H,H,Cl,H,H,H and H,H,H, ,H shown | (blank) |
| E | (blank) | 1-pentyne |
| F | H-C-C-C-H with H,CH3,H and H,OH,H | (blank) |
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: THREE of six correct. Merit: SIX of six correct.

questions.text:
Explain how acidified dichromate solution, Cr2O72-/H+, can be used to distinguish between compounds G and H (below):

| Compound G | Compound H |
|---|---|
| Br | OH |
| CH3-CH2-CH-CH3 | CH3-CH2-CH-CH3 |
| CH3 | CH3 |

In your answer:
- identify the type of reaction occurring
- include conditions required for the reaction to occur
- describe relevant observations
- draw the product formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Acidified dichromate will react with the alcohol group in Compound H (oxidation), but will not react with the haloalkane in Compound G. The orange dichromate solution turns green when heated with Compound H. The product is a ketone.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies type of reaction OR colour change. Merit: Full explanation with reaction type, conditions, observations, and reference to Compound H. Excellence: Full explanation including observation, and reference to BOTH compounds.

questions.text:
Haloalkanes are useful starting materials used in the synthesis of many more complex molecules, including many pharmaceutical products.

Below are some constitutional (structural) isomers of chlorohexane, C6H13Cl. Use these to answer parts (i) to (iii).

Compound G: Cl on a secondary carbon of hexane
Compound I: Cl on a tertiary carbon of 2-methylpentane
Compound J: Cl on a primary carbon of 3-methylpentane
Compound K: Cl on a secondary carbon of 3-methylpentane

Classify each of the haloalkanes as either primary, secondary, or tertiary:

Compound G:
Compound I:
Compound J:
Compound K:
questions.expectedAnswer: Compound G: Secondary. Compound I: Tertiary. Compound J: Primary. Compound K: Secondary.

questions.text:
Compound K forms two different products when reacted with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, KOH(alc), and heat.

Draw both products of the reaction, and circle the correct label (MAJOR / MINOR).
questions.expectedAnswer: Major product: 3-methylpent-2-ene (more substituted alkene, Zaitsev's rule).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies the haloalkane is formed OR correct structures without labels. Merit: Both structures with correct major/minor labels.

questions.text:
Elaborate on the reaction of Compound K with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, KOH(alc), and heat.

In your answer:
- explain why two different products are formed
- justify your choice of major and minor products.
questions.expectedAnswer: Compound K is an unsymmetrical haloalkane, meaning two products can be formed depending upon which adjacent hydrogen is eliminated with the halogen.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Explains why the haloalkane forms two products. Merit: Explains how major/minor products can be identified. Excellence: Justifies why Compound K forms major and minor products, with correct identification.

An incomplete reaction scheme is shown below.

Compound A (2-bromohexane) goes via KOH(alc) heat / Reaction type W to Compound C.

Compound A also goes via NH3(alc) heat / Reaction type Z to Compound B.
Compound E goes via Reagent 4 / Reaction type Y to Compound F and Compound G.

(i) Draw the structural formulae of Compounds B, C, and D in the labelled boxes.

questions.markingGuide: Achievement: FOUR of eight correct. Merit: SIX of eight correct. Excellence: EIGHT of eight correct.

questions.text:
Compound E can be redrawn to enable it to be viewed as a monomer suitable to undergo addition polymerisation.

Draw three repeating units of the polymer that would be produced using the monomer Compound E in the box below.
questions.expectedAnswer: Three repeating units with C-C backbone (single bonds), with appropriate substituent on alternating carbons.

questions.text:
Explain the process of addition polymerisation.

In your answer:
- identify the structure and bonding feature of Compound E that makes it suitable to undergo addition polymerisation
- explain how an addition polymerisation reaction occurs
- compare the relative reactivity of the monomer and the polymer.
questions.expectedAnswer: C=C, carbon to carbon double bond. The double bond breaks open and each monomer unit bonds to the next, forming a long saturated chain. The monomer is more reactive due to the unsaturated C=C bond; the polymer is less reactive due to only having saturated C-C bonds.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Double bond is broken OR identifies polymer is saturated or monomer is unsaturated. Merit: Links saturated/unsaturated nature of polymer/monomer to materials reactivity AND explains addition polymerisation. Excellence: Explains the difference of monomer and polymer in terms of structure and reactivity.

questions.text:
Polypropylene (PP) is a polymer known for use in reusable food containers and automotive parts. Alternatives are being developed that aim to provide similar properties to PP with less environmental impact.

The structure of PP shows repeating units with a CH3 group on alternating carbons of the backbone: -[CH2-CH(CH3)]n-

In the box below, draw the monomer that PP is made from.
questions.expectedAnswer: H2C=CH(CH3) (propene monomer, with C=C double bond and a methyl group).

questions.text:
PP is also used in laboratory equipment such as beakers and centrifuge tubes.

Identify the physical and chemical properties of PP that make it suitable for this use.
questions.expectedAnswer: PP does not melt at moderate temperatures (relatively high melting point for a polymer) and is not chemically reactive with most laboratory reagents.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: States PP has a high melting point OR states that PP is not chemically reactive. Merit: Links PP does not melt at moderate temperatures to use OR links PP is not chemically reactive to use.

questions.text: Draw three straight-chain (non-branched) isomers of C6H13Cl.

Kōrari (flax flower) extract can be processed into various products, as it contains organic acids, such as sinapic and caffeic acids, which have antioxidant properties.

While extracting the kōrari fibre, the following compounds can be isolated:

Ferulic acid (with a carboxylic acid group circled), 1-decanamine (NH2-CH2-(CH2)6-CH3), and 1-hexanamine (NH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3)

Name the functional group circled above.

Explain the procedure you could use to distinguish between 1-decanamine and 1-hexanamine solutions based solely on their physical properties.

Physical properties are limited to differences in melting point, boiling point, and water solubility.

In your answer:
- describe the test method
- compare the observation for each compound
- explain the test result for each compound.
questions.expectedAnswer: 1-decanamine and 1-hexanamine both contain a polar amine group. The longer carbon chain in 1-decanamine makes it less soluble in water and gives it a higher boiling point compared to 1-hexanamine.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Gives a basic method (water/heating). Merit: Explains that chain length will determine which is soluble in water OR explains that chain length determines lower/higher boiling point. Excellence: Fully explains either method, including associated observation, for correct identification and explains relevant carbon chain length effect.

questions.text:
Describe how red and blue litmus paper can be used to distinguish between sinapic acid and 1-decanamine solutions.

Include observations in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Ferulic acid contains a carboxylic acid group and will turn blue litmus red. 1-decanamine contains an amine group and will turn red litmus blue.

questions.text:
Devise an alternative method (without using litmus) to identify the functional group circled in sinapic acid.

In your answer:
- state the reagent needed and the general products formed
- describe the observation, and link to the products formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: The acid reacts with a metal carbonate (e.g. sodium carbonate) in an acid-base reaction, forming a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas (observed as bubbling/effervescence).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: A correct method is described. Merit: A correct method is explained with observations.

questions.text:
Kōrari flowers contain many terpene compounds (volatile organic compounds) that contribute to their scent. An example of a terpene, linalool, is shown below.

Two functional groups (A and B) have been circled. Group A and Group B are both alkene groups (C=C double bonds) but with different substituents.

Identify which of A and B will exist as geometric isomers.
Justify your choice in (b)(i) by explaining the requirements for geometric isomerism.
questions.expectedAnswer: B forms cis/trans isomers, as it has both requirements for geometric isomerism: a C=C double bond preventing free rotation, and each carbon of the double bond has two different groups attached.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies C=C double bond. Merit: Explains why the double bond is required for geometric isomerism AND explains why both C atoms on the double bond must have two different atoms/groups. Excellence: Justifies why B forms geometric isomers, while A does not.
